title: Police clear officer in shooting of homeless man
subtitle: Police recommend mischief charges over claimed cellphone video
article: The external investigation was launched after a Vancouver police officer shot and killed Michael Vann Hubbard, 58, on the 500 block of Homer Street on March 20.
Abbotsford police Insp. Len Georke said the investigators interviewed more than 80 witnesses and watched video recordings from nearby security cameras.
The report concluded Hubbard was holding an X-Acto utility knife, advancing toward two police officers and shouting at them to shoot him when he was shot.
The investigators concluded the confrontation lasted two minutes and 40 seconds, during which time the officers repeatedly backed away as Hubbard continued to approach them.
They also found Hubbard had a history of chronic schizophrenia but toxicology tests found no trace of medications commonly prescribed for the condition in his body.
"The two police officers had reasonable grounds to believe that they were in immediate peril of grievous bodily harm or death," the report concluded.

"After considering the totality of the circumstances facing the two police officers, notwithstanding that there was a tragic outcome, the officers were justified in using force that was intended or likely to cause grievous bodily harm or death," said the report.
The two officers originally confronted Hubbard as part of a search for a suspect in a nearby vehicle break-in. It was later determined that Hubbard was not involved in that incident.
Vancouver police Chief Jim Chu issued a statement Tuesday expressing regret over Hubbard's death, but defending the officers' actions.
"As police officers, we are very aware that it is our job and our duty to safeguard the lives of others as well as our own," said Chu.
"When in the performance of that duty it becomes necessary to take a life, we all share in the sadness of that loss."
The investigation was ordered immediately after the shooting to review the incident and determine if charges should be laid.

While the investigation concluded no charges should be laid against any officers, the investigators did recommend that charges of mischief should be laid against a man who claimed police erased a video recording of the event, which he captured on his cellphone.

Following the incident, Adam Smolcic, 25, told reporters Hubbard was not advancing at the police when he was shot. Attempts by technology experts failed to recover any video from his phone's memory chip.
The report has been forwarded to B.C.'s Police Complaints Commissioner. It is not clear if charges will be laid by the Crown against Smolcic.
Chu was critical both of Smolcic and some news media, who "accepted his allegations and repeated them without critical analysis.
"I would urge those who willingly shoulder the responsibility of public watchdogs to employ their skepticism more widely," Chu said.
